chapter_theme: In the Swayamvara sarukkam, Tivittan's daughter grows up and plays ball with her friends, the parents call the tired girl to them, the father weighs her ripeness, takes counsel and has the swayamvara drum proclaimed, and the kings and the Vidyadhara lords gather round the city.

cast.role: Tivittan's daughter, the maiden of the swayamvara
the mothers and nurses who surround her
her companions and attendants at ball-play
mothers and friends who protest at her play
Tivittan, the dark-hued lord and the girl's father
the king's chief queen, named by rank
the king and queen speaking together
counsellors learned in the science of wealth
the herald who proclaims the swayamvara by drum
the people of the city to whom the herald speaks
the Vidyadhara kings from the silver mountain
the son of Arkkan, who arrives with his lady
the ruler of this mountain who receives him, not named

1747.reading: Bees hum to the flowers and the girl, slender as a flowering creeper, grows up like a great peahen among her mothers and playmates.
1747.nuance: The girl is not named in the verse; she is Tivittan's daughter only from the next verses (1754 calls her the dark-hued one's daughter). Bees and flowers surround her as they do a creeper.
1747.event: The princess grows up amid her mothers and companions.

1748.reading: After a picture of the watery land, with bees, lotus beds, a resting swan and paddy ears like fans, the poet says he now begins the tale of the daughter of that land's lord.
1748.nuance: The land and the girl are paired through the first-person பகருற்றேன் (I begin to tell); the picture of the countryside serves as a frame for her. Printed in 8 half-lines and joined by the build.

1749.reading: The girl, adorned with gold anklets, tiny bells, a fresh silk wrap, a gem girdle and hair curls and head ornaments, joins the crowd of her playmates.
1749.event: The girl, dressed and ornamented, goes to join her playmates.

1750.reading: The young women's ball-play scatters saffron paste, garland pollen and body powder, so that the air turns red like the evening sky.
1750.nuance: The evening-red sky is made by the cosmetics of the players themselves; the game is shown as beauty at its most active.
1750.event: The women play ball and the dust of their ornaments reddens the sky.

1751.reading: The balls in the girls' hands rebound as if alive and, however they are struck, fly up from the jewelled floor and settle on the scented breasts.
1751.nuance: The verse gives the balls a will of their own (ஆவி உடையன போல்), which the next verse turns into a simile of lovers.
1751.event: The balls struck by the women spring back and land on their breasts.

1752.reading: Even when the women strike them away, the balls return to cling to them, like lovers who do harsh things and still will not be restrained.
1752.nuance: Ball-play is read as courtship: the ball plays the lover who is driven off and returns. The comparison is the poet's and does not judge the lover.
1752.event: The women strike the balls and the balls keep returning to them.

1753.reading: The girl tidies her curls, ties her silk wrap and gem girdle, tucks in her gold waist-string, sets her forehead mark straight and takes up the ball.
1753.nuance: She makes herself ready with her own hands before she plays; the same silk and gem girdle dress a bride in 1538, which gives the game a look of rehearsal.
1753.event: The princess dresses herself for play and takes up the ball.

1754.reading: Dark-hued Tivittan's daughter plays ball while her attendants stand with weary hands, her flower-hair, garlands, silk folds, girdle, eyes and arms all swaying with the game.
1754.nuance: The verse names her father by the epithet கார்வண்ணன் (the dark-hued one, Tivittan by the earlier chapters), the first time here that she is placed as his daughter.
1754.event: The princess plays ball while her attendants stand tired beside her.

1755.reading: The balls rise and fall about the sky, the jewelled floor, her silk, girdle and breasts, and the lily-eyed girl, absorbed in the game, cannot make out their coming.
1755.nuance: The last clause, குறிப்பறிய மாட்டாள், can be read as the girl failing to follow where the balls go or failing to read their drift; the second reading would hint at what the game means. Line 4 prints பூங்குழ்லும் for பூங்குழலும்.
1755.event: The princess plays on among the rising and falling balls.

1756.reading: Her mothers and friends stand about her and say that ball-play is no good for her tender body, that her waist will break and her breasts be pressed by her pearl strings, and that the queen or the red-eyed lord would be angry to see it.
1756.nuance: Their worry is for her body and for the anger of her parents (தேவி, செங்கண்மால்), not a rule of conduct; nothing in the verse says the girl stops.
1756.event: Her mothers and friends protest that ball-play is not fit for her.

1757.reading: The dark-hued lord and the queen watch from behind a fine red curtain as she plays like a peahen on a gold floor, and, seeing her tired, call her to come to them.
1757.nuance: The speech is given jointly to the two parents, who watch unseen behind the curtain. Line 6 had a pulli repaired and the stanza was printed in 8 half-lines.
1757.event: The king and queen watch their daughter play and call her to them because she is tired.

1758.reading: At the crowned king's gracious word she lets go of her jewelled ball and, her hair streaming behind, comes and reaches the feet of the dark-lustred one.
1758.nuance: The words அருளிது என்றலும் can be taken as the king's call or as a general phrase of grace; 1757 gives the call. அருமணி முடியவன் and கருமணி ஒளியவன் are read as the same man, Tivittan.
1758.event: At her father's call the princess leaves the game and goes to his feet.

1759.reading: He seats her on his right thigh, wipes the sweat from her brow with his palm and sits in quiet gladness, then looks over her blooming body.
1759.nuance: The father's tenderness and his appraising look sit in one verse: the sweat he wipes comes from the ball-play, and the look prepares the decision of 1762.
1759.event: Tivittan seats his daughter on his lap, wipes her brow and looks at her.

1760.reading: Seeing her young breasts, her richness of form and the beauty of her figure, he feels a joy that makes his heart sigh.
1760.nuance: உளமயா உயிர்ப்பதோர் உவகை can be read as joy that makes the heart sigh, a mixture of pride and anxiety at her ripeness, or as a plain sigh of gladness; the verse does not say a marriage is in his mind, but 1762 follows.
1760.event: The lily-garlanded father sees that his daughter has come of age.

1761.reading: He arranges her fine hair, sets her happily on the queen's lap and goes off to the council-hall of the palace.
1761.nuance: The mantra-sala (மந்திர சாலை மண்டபம்) is a room for counsel, not for ritual; the next verse shows what he does there.
1761.event: Tivittan sets his daughter in the queen's lap and goes to the council hall.

1762.reading: After counsel with men of the science of wealth, whose view agrees with his own, the king commands that the swayamvara drum be struck from an elephant's neck.
1762.nuance: The decision is taken in council, with the ministers named by their learning (அருத்தநூல், the policy texts), and not by the father alone.
1762.event: Tivittan takes counsel with his ministers and orders the swayamvara drum proclaimed.

claims.claim: a king settles a weighty matter after counsel with those who know the science of policy

1763.reading: The drum, smeared with white sandal paste and hung with peacock-feather garlands, is struck with a roar like hail.
1763.nuance: This is the drum that receives offerings (பலிபெறு முரசம்); its sound announces the wedding to everyone.

1764.reading: A herald calls for the king's long life, the earth's welfare, enemies sunk, virtue spreading, cool rain, ripe crops and grief brought low, and bids the people hear the proclamation.
1764.nuance: The blessing runs from the king through the country's rain and harvest and its virtue; the ruler stands at the head of every wish, as in the Kural's picture of just rule.
1764.event: The herald opens the proclamation with blessings on the king and land.

1765.reading: The herald bids the people decorate the city of the forest-ringed gold town, raise festival arches, welcome white festival dress and honour guests, and put flowers and vessels in order.
1765.event: The herald orders the city decorated and guests honoured.

1766.reading: The thunderous drum is said to have declared that the swayamvara is fixed for ten days from today and that the world should gather with the kings who live in concord.
1766.nuance: ஈரைஞ் ஞாள் is read as ten days counting today; the verse closes with என்பவே (they say), so the narrator reports the proclamation at a remove.
1766.event: The drum announces the swayamvara for ten days later and summons the kings.

1767.reading: The drum thunders through the royal city's streets like a cloud-burst, and the peacocks in the mansions, taking it for rain, are bewildered.
1767.nuance: Peacocks that mistake the drum for rain-clouds belong to the poet's stock of images; the whole city is shown shaken by the news.

1768.reading: With drums, conches and heavy armies, kings and those who are not kings pour like the sea round the city and fill the outer ring of its wall.
1768.nuance: The line names both kings and non-kings (அரசரல்லாரும்), so the crowd is more than suitors: those who come to watch are counted too.
1768.event: Kings and others arrive in force and surround the city walls.

1769.reading: The Vidyadhara kings from the silver mountain, with sea-like armies and a blinding radiance, come and camp among the eight mountains.
1769.nuance: எண்மலைச் சிலம்பு (the slopes of the eight mountains) is hard to place; the verse likely means the camp-ground outside the city.
1769.event: The Vidyadhara kings arrive with their armies and encamp.

1770.reading: The son of Arkkan, who is lord of that mountain's kings, comes with a lady with dark long eyes while the ruler of this mountain goes out to greet him.
1770.nuance: The verse does not give his name. Who receives him (இவ்வரை அரைசு) is not stated: it may be Tivittan or a kinsman of the city. Line 4 prints அரைசெதிர் for அரைசு எதிர்.
1770.event: Arkkan's son arrives with his lady and is received by the local ruler.

links.note: 1752 likens the returning balls to lovers who will not be held off; Thiruppugazh 586 asks Murugan not to let the poet waste away over women whose palms ache from ball-play.
links.teaches: One text enjoys ball-play as courtship, and the other treats the same game as the snare from which a devotee asks to be freed.

gains.a: The epic's lively ball-play gains the devotee's view that this very beauty is what he must be saved from.
gains.b: The Thiruppugazh's brief mention of ball-playing women gains a full scene of what the game is, with its clinging balls and flying powder.

links.note: 1538 has attendants tie the bride's fine cloth and gem girdle for the wedding; 1753 has her daughter tie the same silk and gem girdle for ball-play.
links.teaches: The girl's self-dressing repeats her mother's bridal dressing and shows the game as a step toward marriage.

links.note: 1757 has the parents call the tired daughter from behind the curtain; 1758 shows her letting the ball go and reaching her father's feet.
links.teaches: The call becomes obedience: the daughter breaks off her play at once, which is how a swayamvara's choice is later left to the father's council.

links.note: 1759 has the father hold his sweat-brow daughter after ball-play; Akananuru 17 recalls a girl too tired for a ball game who lay in her mother's arms.
links.teaches: The tired child resting in a parent's arms is the last scene before she leaves for a husband, by public choice in the epic and by flight in the akam poem.

gains.a: The epic's scene of the father holding his daughter gains the foreboding of loss that the akam poem builds from the same picture.
gains.b: The foster mother's memory gains a case where the father arranges the girl's marriage openly, which the elopement she mourns has bypassed.

links.note: 1760 shows the father seeing his daughter's ripening body; 1762 follows with a council that sets the swayamvara.
links.teaches: Her ripeness is the unspoken cause of the proclamation: the poem lets the father's look become public policy.

links.note: 1762 has the king command the drum after council; 1763 has the drum struck.
links.teaches: The order given in the council is carried out at once in public sound.

links.note: 1763 beats a drum to announce a wedding; Naladiyar 23 says the drums that sounded for a wedding may sound the same day as funeral drums.
links.teaches: The same drum that proclaims joy is, for the Naladiyar, the sign of how quickly joy passes into death.

gains.a: The epic's wedding drum gains a shadow: the sound that calls the kings is the sound a worldly man should fear.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the wedding drum is proclaimed with royal pomp for a bride not yet chosen.

links.note: 1764's herald prays for the king's life, virtue and cool rain and harvest; Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather where the ruler wields his sceptre justly.
links.teaches: The herald's prayer asks for the rain and crops that the Kural says come as a fruit of just rule, so the blessing doubles as a claim on the king.

gains.a: The herald's list of blessings gains a rule: rain and crops are the sign that the king's sceptre is just.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ceremony in which this wish is spoken aloud as the king's reign is made public.

links.note: 1766 has the drum summon the world's kings to a marriage open to all; Naladiyar 86 praises a wife married with drums beaten for many to know.
links.teaches: A marriage announced to all is a mark of honour in the Naladiyar, and the swayamvara pushes the same openness to where the bride is chosen before the world.

gains.a: The proclamation gains a measure: public marriage is thought to guard the bond from later claims.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the drum summons rival suitors as well as witnesses.

links.note: 1766 has the drum fix the day and call the kings; 1768 shows kings and others arriving round the city.
links.teaches: The proclamation is answered by the arrival, and the crowd outruns the invited kings.

source_issues: Verses 1748-1757 and 1759? were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four lines by the build; read as four.
1757 line 6 had a pulli after a vowel sign removed by the build.
1770 line 4 prints அரைசெதிர் for அரைசு எதிர்; the receiver of Arkkan's son is not named.
